720	After they finished the Shas three times, they didn't know
721	a single word — not a word — they didn't know Hebrew,
722	they learned Hebrew, they learned Aramaic, they learned
723	the Gemaras,
724	they ended their lives, they ended their lives
725	having completed the Shas three times,
726	and so they went to their world. One story: the son of one of them says
727	that he remembers his father, how suddenly his father,
728	suddenly at the age of 70, took it upon himself.
729	And I agreed with him, I took him and we began. It was very hard
730	until he learned the first two pages, but
731	afterward he began to swim in the Gemara at 70, and then
732	he completed the Shas three times. When he finished the Shas,
733	only a few days after completing the Shas three times,
734	with all the grandchildren, great-grandchildren, family and friends
735	sitting at his siyum, only a few days later
736	he passed away to eternal life in the World to Come. You see, it depends on will,
737	it depends on a person's will.
738	And this is what it says: "It is possible that his evil is visible and revealed,
739	while his good is hidden and concealed.
740	And I, on the contrary — he is worthy of the Almighty's mercy
741	and atonement more than I am. One merit of his weighs
742	more than many of my merits."
743	He says: the good deed is hidden, because no one observes it
744	except the Creator, blessed be He, and people don't praise him for it
745	and he is not honored for it. And I, on the contrary, since what is seen
746	of mine is better than what is seen of his. And so, the more
747	a person conceals things — "the glory of Elokim is to conceal a matter" — the more a person can
748	hide things, details, of mitzvot, of
749	good deeds, the greater the glory of Elokim: concealing a matter,
750	this is only between me and the Holy One, blessed be He.
751	And likewise, regarding sins: one sin of mine
752	weighs as many sins,
753	because I know exactly that it is a sin, since I committed it
754	in hiding and secrecy. And his sin is visible and publicized,
755	people denounce him for it, they come
756	and condemn him, they shame him.
757	He will rejoice,
758	his reward for the deed in this world will be reduced because of the publicity,
759	and his reward will remain for him in the World to Come, and his punishment
760	for the sin in this world will be reduced because people condemn him
761	for it,
762	while the punishment for my sins will remain for the World to Come, Heaven
763	forbid.
764	And furthermore, when I set my heart to examine people's flaws,
765	to look into their bad character traits —
766	look into my own shortcomings instead. Do not look
767	at the flaw in you, do not tell your friend. Do not look into others' flaws,
768	look into your own flaws.
769	"If I am not for myself, who is for me?"
770	It is forbidden for a person to look into another's flaws.
771	Of course you may rebuke — "you shall surely rebuke your fellow, and not
772	bear sin because of him." We have a principle that a person is forbidden
773	to take up people's sins. But he should know everything,
774	know that everything is counted and finished before the Creator of worlds,
775	everything is accounted for. And a person's reward — how
776	does the Rabbi write here, the Pele Yoetz? We said we would say
777	this, the Pele Yoetz. It is a merit for a person
778	to read his holy words.
779	To read his holy words — a few words.
780	The Pele Yoetz said to a person: he gave us, yes,
781	more than 500...
782	these are sets that we will study. So I will say
783	a few things here about the mitzvah of tzedakah, how the evil inclination stands
784	against a person,
785	stands against a person: "What, suddenly you give? Why do you
786	give? Why tzedakah?" How far does its power extend —
787	it is beyond words.
788	Already there is a book composed, Ma'yil Tzedakah, by Rabbi Eliyahu
789	HaCohen of Izmir,
790	about
791	250, 300 years ago. He writes wondrous things there.
792	He composed two parts, Ma'yil Tzedakah. What is
793	this matter? How much a person must strive in order
794	to merit being a giver of tzedakah at all times. He already
795	composed a book on tzedakah, a rod of mussar, and a pure man gathered all
796	the statements of our Sages in the Shas and Midrashim that speak in praise of
797	great goodness, and according to its greatness and goodness,
798	a person's inclination overpowers him: "What do you mean? Not you,
799	you don't need to give them, what will become of them? No,
800	you yourself need it, what are you talking about?"
801	His evil inclination hardens his heart
802	so that he won't do it, so that he doesn't act. And about
803	this they said in Eruvin: a person is recognized by his pocket.
804	A person who merits
805	to be generous of heart,
806	open —
807	what we call "generous" — gives in a
808	broad way, and is happy to give, not pained; on the contrary, he has
809	joy. Because, I told him, "Listen, this is a
810	big sum, what are you doing?" I said to him, "Yes, it
811	seems to me this is a big sum."
812	He tells me, "What do you want to say to me? This is what
813	will remain for me. This is what will stay with me. Everything else I
814	will leave here." That's what he tells me. "Everything I
815	will leave. One thing I take with me. So as much
816	as I can invest, I will invest in this."
817	Ah,
818	how great is his goodness, how great his portion! How pleasant his lot
819	in this world and in the World to Come! "Wealth and riches." A person
820	thinks, "If I give, then I... listen, in my house
821	I won't have."
822	The more you give, the more you will have in your house. So
823	this is the rule: "Aser te'aser" — you tithe, know that you
824	will become rich.
825	You will merit it. A person tithes from his money, yes, tithes
826	without a vow — he says, "This tithe I
827	distribute, distribute, distribute to this one, to that one, here," and also from time to
828	time he keeps some savings of tithes to give, and
829	suddenly there is some big tzedakah, baruch HaShem.

831	and riches are in his house, and his righteousness stands forever." And behold, this is
832	a sharp merchant,
833	"who lends to HaShem," a loan. Why?
